title: DBMS Architecture & Data Abstraction
summary: How a DBMS hides messy storage behind clean layers, so you can change the disk without breaking the app. The three-schema idea and the languages that drive it.

blocks.markdown:
A DBMS hides *how* data is stored behind clean layers, so apps ask **what** they want, not **where** it lives.

- Splits the system into **three levels**: physical, logical, and view.
- This separation is called **data abstraction** — the plumbing stays hidden.
- It buys **data independence**: change storage without rewriting apps.
- Everything is driven by DB **languages** (DDL, DML, DCL, TCL).

blocks.subTitle: The three levels at a glance
blocks.markdown:
One database, seen at three heights.

| Level | Answers |
|---|---|
| Physical | How bytes sit on disk |
| Logical | What tables and columns exist |
| View | What one user is allowed to see |

Apps live at the view/logical levels and never touch the physical one.

blocks.subTitle: The big picture
blocks.markdown:
The classic **ANSI/SPARC three-schema** design stacks the levels.

<<< Image: A clean vertical stack diagram, 3 rounded boxes, blue/grey palette, generous whitespace. Top box 'External / View level (per-user views)', middle box 'Conceptual / Logical level (all tables, constraints)', bottom box 'Internal / Physical level (files, indexes, bytes on disk)'. A short arrow labelled 'logical data independence' between top and middle; a short arrow labelled 'physical data independence' between middle and bottom. 2-3 word labels only. >>>

- **External** — many tailored views, one per user or app.
- **Conceptual** — the single logical schema of the whole database.
- **Internal** — the physical storage details.

blocks.subTitle: What each level does
blocks.markdown:
Reading the stack top to bottom:

- **View (external)** — hides columns a user shouldn't see; a sales rep sees orders, not salaries.
- **Logical (conceptual)** — the true design: tables, columns, keys, and constraints. This is where you model.
- **Physical (internal)** — page layout, file organization, and which indexes exist.

Designers spend their time at the **logical** level; the DBMS handles the physical one.

**Data independence** = change one level without touching the level above. That is the whole payoff of the layers.

| Kind | Change made | App impact |
|---|---|---|
| Physical | New index, new disk layout | None |
| Logical | Add a column or table | Ideally none |

Physical independence is easy and near-total; logical independence is harder because apps depend on the schema shape.

Two words that sound similar but aren't.

- **Schema** — the *design*: the tables, columns, and types. Changes rarely. Think of it as the blueprint.
- **Instance** — the *data* in the database right now. Changes constantly with every insert and delete.

One schema, endless instances over time — like a class versus its objects.

blocks.subTitle: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL
blocks.markdown:
SQL is really four sub-languages doing different jobs.

| Family | Job | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| DDL | Define structure | CREATE, ALTER, DROP |
| DML | Move data | INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE |
| DCL | Grant access | GRANT, REVOKE |
| TCL | Bound transactions | COMMIT, ROLLBACK |

SELECT (querying) is often called DQL, a slice of DML.

blocks.subTitle: One line of each
blocks.markdown:
The four families in four statements:

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);  -- DDL
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'Ada');                 -- DML
GRANT SELECT ON users TO analyst;                    -- DCL
COMMIT;                                              -- TCL
```

- DDL shapes the container, DML fills it, DCL guards it, TCL makes changes permanent.

blocks.subTitle: The engine's main parts
blocks.markdown:
Zooming into the physical level, a DBMS engine has a few managers.

- **Query processor** — parses SQL and picks an execution plan.
- **Storage manager** — handles files, pages, and the buffer pool in RAM.
- **Transaction manager** — enforces ACID via locks and the log.
- **Catalog** — the metadata store describing every table (the schema itself).

We open the storage engine fully in [storage-file-organization](storage-file-organization).

blocks.subTitle: Where the DBMS runs
blocks.markdown:
Physically, a database is usually reached across tiers.

- **Two-tier** — app talks straight to the DBMS (a desktop tool, a simple service).
- **Three-tier** — browser to app server to DBMS; the DB never faces the internet directly.

The three-tier shape is the norm for web apps because it isolates and protects the database.

Where people trip on the concepts:

- **Confusing schema with instance.** Adding a row does not change the schema; adding a column does.
- **Assuming full logical independence.** Apps hard-code column names, so schema changes often *do* ripple.
- **Thinking a view stores data.** A view is a saved query over real tables, not a copy.
- **Ignoring the catalog.** The DBMS reads its own metadata tables on every query.

blocks.subTitle: Three-schema architecture
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Explain the three-schema architecture.**

A DBMS defines three levels: **Internal** (how data is physically stored), **Conceptual** (the logical design of all tables and constraints), and **External** (tailored views per user or app). Apps see only their view and never touch storage. This is the ANSI/SPARC three-schema model.

blocks.subTitle: Physical vs logical data independence
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Physical vs logical data independence — what's the difference?**

**Physical independence** means you can change storage (new index, new disk) without touching the logical schema or apps. **Logical independence** means you can change the logical schema (add a table) without rewriting external views. Physical is easy; logical is harder because apps often depend on exact column names.

blocks.subTitle: Schema vs instance
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Schema vs instance — give an example.**

The **schema** is the blueprint: `CREATE TABLE users (id INT, name TEXT)`. The **instance** is the actual data right now: the rows in that table. Schema changes rarely (a migration); instances change on every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE.

blocks.subTitle: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What are DDL, DML, DCL, and TCL?**

**DDL** (CREATE/ALTER/DROP) defines structure. **DML** (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) moves data. **DCL** (GRANT/REVOKE) controls access. **TCL** (COMMIT/ROLLBACK) manages transactions. SELECT is sometimes called DQL. In practice they are all written in SQL; the split is conceptual.

blocks.subTitle: DBMS engine components
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Name the main components inside a DBMS engine.**

**Query processor** — parses and optimizes SQL. **Storage manager** — reads/writes pages on disk and manages the buffer pool. **Transaction manager** — enforces ACID with locks and a write-ahead log. **Catalog** — system tables that store the schema itself.
